cards.question: List what you should be wearing when riding in the countryside or leading a pony on the road; explain why each item on your list is important
cards.answer:
* A current-standard, correctly fitted riding hat protects your head. 
 * Secure boots with a defined heel protect your feet 
 * gloves improve grip and protect your hands. 
 * Wear bright or reflective clothing so other road users can see you 
 * suitable outerwear keeps you safe for the weather.

cards.question: Show how to work safely with a pony when dismounted
cards.answer:
Approach calmly where the pony can see or hear you and speak before touching. 
 * Wear suitable footwear, use a correctly fitted headcollar and lead rope, and never wrap the rope around your hand. 
 * Wear suitable footwear, use a correctly fitted headcollar and lead rope, and never wrap the rope around your hand.

cards.question: Explain how you would ride in the countryside and on bridle paths, showing an awareness of farmers’ stock and crops
cards.answer:
Important: 
 Never ride on land without permission (unless it is your own land). Trespassing is against the law and you may be prosecuted. 

 Countryside: 
 * Always be courteous to other countryside users. 
 * Always walk past (not trot or canter) as some people are frightened by ponies. 
 * If it is wet you may splash people with water, or mud, if you trot or canter past. 
 * Take care not to disturb wildlife, or ride over wild flowers. 
 * Approach other riders slowly and ask permission to go past if you are riding more quickly. 

 Farmland: 
 * Some bridleways may cross farmland. 
 * Some farmers may let you ride across their land (without bridleways) if you ask permission first. 
 * Keep to the edge of the crops and always close the gates behind you (if animals are in the fields, or if you had to open the gate to pass through). 
 * Always walk through fields with livestock, not trot or canter. 
 * Do not ride through the middle of hers of livestock. 
 * If cows or sheep are curious and come towards you, keep your pony walking steadily forward so they do not become frightened. Do not canter or gallop as cows may chase you.

cards.question: Explain how positive reinforcement works when training a pony
Talk about how pressure and release works when training a pony (this is negative reinforcement)
Describe how you could get a pony used to something scary (desensitisation)
cards.answer:
Desensitisation describes how you gradually get a pony to accept something they find scary, are unsure of, or which might frighten them. 

 Desensitisation occurs when a pony is gradually allowed to get used to something that worries them over a period of time. 

 The process of desensitisation should be done in very small steps so that the pony gets used to, and is confident with one step before you introduce the next one. 

 Stop each session before the pony becomes stressed, or uncomfortable. Proceed through the steps over several days, not rushing the pony. 

 Reward the pony when they accept each step so that they know they have done well.

cards.question: Understand that ponies are herd animals; give an example of when this might be a problem and how you might avoid it
Describe some of the things that a pony might do if it is in pain, frightened, or insufficiently trained
cards.answer:
Pain: When ponies have pain somewhere in their body they may change the way they behave, or the way they move. 
 Ponies are very good at hiding signs that they are in pain as in the wild this makes them more vulnerable to predators. 
 Signs that a pony is in pain can be: 
 * Limp if pain is in their foot, leg, joints, shoulders, hips or back 
 * Take un-level steps 
 * Carry their head to one side 
 * Appear crooked when they move 
 * Their posture may be tense and their back arched 
 * Keep getting down to roll if the pain is in their stomach 
 * Kick out after a jump 
 * Keep looking at or kicking their stomach if it hurts 
 * Buck, or carry their head abnormally high if ridden with a badly fitting saddle or when they have back pain 
 * Take off suddenly due to a spasm of pain 
 * Their facial expression may change: their jaw may be tense, their eyes stare, their ears back and their nostrils flared 
 * Their nostrils may change shape and be more closed 
 * The skin around their eyes may become wrinkled and their eye appear less open. 

 Frightened: The natural reaction of a pony to something that frightens them is to take flight and run away to get as far away as possible from the scary thing. 
 Different things frighten different ponies and they will only fight if they have nowhere to run and cannot escape. 
 Ponies can fight by bucking, rearing, biting and kicking. 
 Signs that a pony is frightened are: 
 * Wide eyes 
 * Flare nostrils 
 * Snorting, breathing heavily 
 * Bracing their neck and high head carriage 
 * Clamping their tail to their hindquarters 
 * Shaking 
 * Unable to stay calm or stand still 
 * Chewing the bit to relieve anxiety 

 Insufficiently trained: 
 Ponies are not naughty on purpose. Most of what we think of as _naughty_ behaviour is because they do not understand what we are asking them to do, or we are not giving clear aids, or commands. 
 Insufficiently trained ponies may appear to be: 
 * Lazy 
 * Stubborn 
 * Difficult to train

cards.question: Present to the test in safe, tidy turn out
Check bridle, saddle, girth, and stirrups before mounting
Mount and dismount correctly on both sides, using a mounting block
Hold the reins correctly and at a suitable length for the work being done
Ride with stirrups of a suitable length
Alter stirrups when mounted
Tighten girth when mounted
Be working towards a balanced seat, independent of the reins
cards.answer:
Key building blocks for demonstrating this ability are: 
 * Not pulling, leaning or balancing on the pony mouth via the reins 
 * Absorbing the movement of the pony through supple joints (knees, hips, ankles) without gripping or bouncing 
 * Stability in walk 

 At D+ level the Riding Skills tested may include: 
 * Walk without stirrups 
 * Walk on loose rein and shorten the reins 
 * Simple turns and circles in walk and trot 
 * Control of a quiet pony in company on roads, and in the countryside 
 * Ride up and down hills in walk 
 * Canter, single pole and very small fence 

 At C level the same Riding Skills are tested but assessors will look for: 
 * Higher degree of control and harmony 
 * Correct application of simple aids 
 * Safe riding on roads and in the countryside.

cards.question: Use legs and hands as aids to increase and decrease pace
cards.answer:
Riders should use seat, legs and hand aids independently and in coordination. 
 Independent means relaxed, open joints that follow the horses movements. 
 Coordination means that the aids (hands, legs, seat) are matching the movements of the pony. 

 At D or D+ test level a rider is expected to: 
 * Show basic use of legs aids to go forward 
 * Maintain control of a quiet pony around other ponies 

 At C test level a rider is also expected to: 
 * ride in balance without relying on the reins 
 * Direct transitions using leg and hand aids to increase and decrease pace. 

 At C+ test level a rider is also expected to: 
 * Apply aids correctly for balanced transitions, including changes of leg at canter through to trot 
 * Discuss the horse response to aids, rhythm, tempo and suppleness

cards.question: Show the difference between walking on a contact and on a long rein
Ride in balance without stirrups in walk and trot
Explain the difference between rhythm and tempo
Describe the sequence of legs in walk, trot, canter, and gallop (these are the footfalls)
Show trot and canter in a balanced light seat with stirrups at a suitable length
Ride in a correct, balanced position in walk and trot over poles on the ground
Ride in a correct, balanced position over small fences (maximum height, 60 cm)
Show a smooth progression from one fence to the next
Know the correct distances for trotting poles (in feet, yard or metres) for the pony you are riding
Ride safely in closed and open order in a group
Ride independently in the open; explain why this might be a problem for a herd animal and suggest a solution
Ride up and down hills in walk and trot in suitable balance
List what you should be wearing when riding in the countryside or leading a pony on the road; explain why each item on your list is important
Show how to work safely with a pony when dismounted
Show, and understand the importance of, the correct way of lifting objects in general use around the stable yard (e.g., feed and water buckets) safely
cards.answer:
When moving, or lifting, heavy objects always consider your own safety and that of anyone helping you. Always take bales from the top of the stack so that the stack does not collapse on you, and carry water buckets two at a time (and not overfilled) so that your body is balanced. 

 How to lift heavy objects: 
 * Wear gloves to protect your hands and give you a secure grip 
 * Stand close to the heavy object with your feet apart to help maintain your balance 
 * Square the object (e.g. bale or sack) up in front of you 
 * Tuck in your chin 
 * Bend your knees keeping your sprint straight. Do not bend forward over heavy objects as this will strain your back. 
 * Keep your arms close to your body and lift by straightening your knees, not by using the strength in your arms, or back. 

 Putting down heavy objects: 
 * Keep the object close to your body 
 * Keep your chin tucked in 
 * Bend your knees 
 * Lower the object to the ground 
 * Let go and stand up normally. 

 Heavy objects should always be moved around the yard using a wheel barrow, or sack barrow, rather than being carried from one point to another, or by being dragged across the ground.

cards.question: List and explain the importance of the Five Domains of pony welfare
cards.answer:
Nutrition: suitable food and water. 
 * Physical environment: comfortable, safe surroundings. 
 * Health: protection from pain, injury and disease. 
 * Behavioural interactions: movement, choice and suitable contact with horses, people and the environment. 
 * Mental state: the positive and negative experiences produced by the other four domains.

cards.question:
Give two examples of the physical/mental effects on ponies of:
a) Poor feeding and watering
cards.answer:
a) Poor feeding and watering can: 
 Cause hunger, thirst, weakness, weight loss or poor condition. 
 Increase the risk of colic, gastric irritation, laminitis or other illness. 
 Create stress, frustration, poor concentration or unwanted behaviour.

cards.question:
Give two examples of the physical/mental effects on ponies of:
 b) Good paddocks and stables
cards.answer:
b) Good Paddocks: 
 provide safe footing, shelter, ventilation, clean water and freedom from avoidable hazards. 
 support rest, movement, grazing and appropriate contact with other horses. 
 are a comfortable environment helps the pony feel secure and reduces injury and illness risk.

cards.question:
Give two examples of the physical/mental effects on ponies of: 
c) Poor health (including the effects of injuries and pain)
cards.answer:
c) Poor health: 
 The pony may move unevenly, rest a limb, become reluctant or change posture. 
 It may eat less, lose condition, seem dull or become unusually defensive. 
 Ongoing pain causes fear or distress and must be investigated promptly

cards.question:
Give two examples of the physical/mental effects on ponies of:
d) Being unable to behave in a natural way
cards.answer:
d) Unable to behave in a natural way can cause: 
 Lack of movement, forage, choice or social contact can cause boredom, frustration and stress. 
 The pony may call, barge, become withdrawn or develop stereotypes such as weaving or box-walking. 
 Provide turnout, forage, companionship, exercise and safe opportunities to explore and choose.

cards.question:
Give two examples of the physical/mental effects on ponies of: 
e) Being scared (e.g., of people or other animals)
cards.answer:
e) Being scared can cause: 
 Raised head, tense muscles, wide eyes, flared nostrils, rapid breathing or sweating. 
 Freezing, shying, rushing, spinning, barging or trying to escape. 
 Repeated fear can reduce trust and learning; find the cause and make the situation safer and easier.

cards.question: Explain how positive reinforcement works when training a pony
cards.answer:
* It means adding something the pony values immediately after the wanted behaviour. 
 * Example: the pony stands quietly; you give a scratch or small food reward straight away. 
 * This makes the correct behaviour more likely to happen again.

cards.question: Talk about how pressure and release works when training a pony (this is negative reinforcement)
cards.answer:
* Apply the lightest suitable pressure to ask for a response. 
 * The instant the pony gives the correct response, remove the pressure. 
 * Example: light lead-rope pressure asks the pony to step forward; release immediately when it steps.

cards.question: Understand that ponies are herd animals; give an example of when this might be a problem and how you might avoid it
cards.answer:
* Ponies naturally look to other horses for companionship and safety. 
 * Separation may cause calling, rushing, barging or attempts to follow another pony. 
 * Practise separation gradually, use secure handling and avoid unexpectedly leaving a pony alone.

cards.question: Explain how to care for and work a pony that lives out at grass
cards.answer:
CARE: 
 * Check the pony at least daily—preferably twice—for health, injury, movement, condition and all four feet. 
 * Provide safe fencing, clean water, suitable grazing or forage, shelter and companionship. 
 * Maintain farriery, dentistry, vaccinations and a veterinary-led parasite-control plan. 

 WORK 
 * Exercise should suit age, health, condition and fitness, increasing gradually. 
 * Check feet, legs and tack before work; allow warm-up, cool-down, water and recovery. 
 * Adjust work for weather, ground and grazing condition, and stop if the pony is tired, sore or unwell.

cards.question: Know the main signs of health in the pony; recognise when a pony is too fat or too thin
cards.answer:
HEALTH 
 * Bright, alert and interested, with a normal appetite and drinking pattern. 
 * Clear eyes and nostrils, healthy coat and skin, normal droppings and urine. 
 * Moves soundly, bears weight evenly and has normal temperature, pulse and breathing for that pony. 

 BODY CONDITION 
 * Look and feel the neck, shoulders, ribs, spine, loin and quarters—do not judge by the belly alone. 
 * Too thin: ribs, spine or pelvis are too easy to see or feel and muscle may be poor. 
 * Too fat: ribs are difficult to feel, with fat pads on the crest, shoulders, back or tail head.

cards.question: Discuss how to check whether a paddock is safe
cards.answer:
* Secure fencing and gates, with no sharp edges, loose wire, holes or trapped areas. 
 * Clean working water supply, suitable shelter and safe footing without dangerous mud or ice. 
 * No poisonous plants, rubbish, machinery or unsafe livestock; grazing must suit the pony and group. 

 Daily checks should include: 
 Water, fencing and gates; shelter and ground conditions. 
 * Poisonous plants, fallen branches, litter, holes and other new hazards. 
 * Droppings, grass availability and whether every pony in the group can safely access resources.

cards.question: Explain elementary rules of feeding and watering
cards.answer:
FEEDING 
 * Base the diet on forage and feed according to bodyweight, condition, workload, age and health. 
 * Make changes gradually; feed little and often and keep meal times consistent. 
 * Use clean, good-quality feed, weigh rations, keep utensils clean and allow time after a large feed before hard work. 

 WATERING 
 * Provide unlimited clean, fresh water and check buckets or troughs every day 
 * Offer water before and after work and during longer journeys; do not deliberately withhold it. 
 * Monitor changes in drinking because they may indicate illness or a supply problem.

cards.question: Show when to use positive rewards (food, scratching) when training a pony for stable manners
cards.answer:
* Choose one clear behaviour, such as standing quietly or moving back from the door. 
 * Mark and reward the correct response immediately with a scratch or small food reward. 
 * Deliver food safely away from your body and stop if the pony becomes muggy; be consistent.

cards.question: How do you groom a grass kept pony
cards.answer:
* Secure the pony safely and check the whole body for heat, swelling, wounds, skin problems and ticks. 
 * Pick out all four feet; remove loose mud with suitable brushes without stripping useful coat oils unnecessarily. 
 * Be gentle over sensitive areas and avoid over-grooming a pony that relies on its natural weather protection.

cards.question: Put on a tail bandage
cards.answer:
* The tail and bandage must be clean and dry; use even overlap and even pressure from top to bottom. 
 * It must be secure but never tight, with no wrinkles or pressure points. 
 * Check it frequently and never leave it on longer than necessary; remove immediately if there is swelling or discomfort.

cards.question: Know when a pony needs shoeing
cards.answer:
* Overgrown, unbalanced or cracked feet; flares, chips or altered movement. 
 * A shoe may be loose, worn or twisted, with raised clenches, missing nails or hoof growth beyond it. 
 * Keep regular farrier appointments and contact the farrier promptly rather than waiting for a shoe to come off.

cards.question: Put on and take off turn out rugs
cards.answer:
[YouTube video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L3O4tSzrE1I) on The Pony Club channel for Putting on Rugs 
 
 * Check the rug is the right type, size, clean and undamaged; keep control of the pony. 
 * Put on: position the rug, fasten chest first, then surcingles and finally leg or fillet straps. 
 * Remove in reverse order—leg/fillet straps, surcingles, then chest—before sliding it back and off calmly. 
 *  It should sit in front of the withers without pressure, slipping or pulling backwards. 
 * Shoulders must move freely; chest fastenings should not gape, pinch or rub. 
 * Surcingles should cross with safe clearance beneath the belly and straps must be correctly arranged.

cards.question: Put on a saddle, saddle cloth, bridle, and martingale
cards.answer: [YouTube video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IN88Jp5tRKA) for B test training from Sasha Hargreaves covering correct methods of putting on saddle, bridle and martingale

cards.question: Have some knowledge of correctly fitting tack (saddle clearing the withers; height of the bit; noseband tightness)
cards.answer:
* The headpiece and browband should not pinch the ears; cheekpieces hold the bit evenly at a suitable height. 
 * The noseband must be correctly positioned with enough space—commonly checked as two fingers over the nasal bone. 
 * The throatlash, reins and fastenings must be secure without restricting breathing, swallowing or jaw movement. 
 * The cloth is clean, flat and pulled into the gullet with no wrinkles. 
 * The saddle sits level and balanced, clears the withers and spine, and does not rock or pinch. 
 * The girth and straps are sound and correctly fastened; fit should be checked regularly by a qualified saddle fitter. 
 * The neck and centre straps must lie safely without restricting the shoulders or pulling the saddle. 
 * When raised, the rings should reach approximately to the top of the withers; the reins pass through both rings. 
 * Rein stops are essential between the rings and the bit, and the martingale must not force the head down.

cards.question: Talk about elementary care and cleaning of saddlery (tack care after daily exercise)
cards.answer:
* Wipe away sweat, mud and grease; clean the bit separately with clean water. 
 * Clean leather with suitable products and allow damp tack to dry naturally away from direct heat. 
 * Check stitching, buckles, reins, girth straps and stirrup leathers, then store tack safely and neatly.

cards.question: Know how to clean a minor wound
cards.answer:
* First make the pony and handler safe and assess the wound. 
 * Gently flush dirt away with plenty of clean water or sterile saline; use clean hands and materials. 
 * Do not scrub deeply or apply powders and creams unless advised; monitor for heat, swelling, pain or discharge.

cards.question: Know which wounds require veterinary attention
cards.answer:
* Deep, gaping, puncture or heavily contaminated wounds and uncontrolled bleeding. 
 * Wounds near an eye, joint, tendon sheath, chest or abdomen, or those with an embedded object. 
 * Call for lameness, severe pain, shock, infection or uncertainty; check tetanus vaccination status.

cards.question:
Understand the reasons for routine healthcare:
a) Equine influenza and tetanus vaccinations
b) Dental care
cards.answer:
Equine Influenza: 
 * Equine influenza is highly contagious and causes fever, coughing, nasal discharge and poor performance. 
 * Vaccination reduces the risk and severity of disease and helps limit spread. 
 * Follow the current Pony Club activity rules and the vet vaccination schedule. 

 Tetanus: 
 * Tetanus bacteria can enter through very small wounds and produce a potentially fatal toxin. 
 * Horses are particularly susceptible, but vaccination gives effective protection. 
 * Keep boosters current and ask the vet after a wound if vaccination status is uncertain. 

 Dental Care: 
 * Teeth wear unevenly and sharp points or other problems can cause pain. 
 * Signs include dropping feed, slow eating, cribbing, weight loss, bad breath or resisting the bit. 
 * A vet or qualified equine dental technician should check teeth at intervals suited to the pony.

cards.question: Recognise when a pony is clearly lame
cards.answer:
* Uneven rhythm, shortened stride, reluctance to bear weight or difficulty turning. 
 * In front-leg lameness, the head often rises when the lame leg bears weight and drops on the sound leg. 
 * Stop work, check safely and tell a responsible adult; severe or sudden lameness needs veterinary advice.

cards.question: Recognise signs that a pony might be unhappy (stressed, worried or anxious)
cards.answer:
* Tense posture, fixed stare, tight lips, flared nostrils, rapid breathing or sweating. 
 * Calling, pawing, rushing, barging, tail swishing, reluctance to eat or withdrawal. 
 * Repeated weaving, box-walking or crib-biting can signal a welfare problem; investigate the cause.

cards.question: Understand the means of protecting a pony’s legs while travelling
cards.answer:
* Use well-fitting travel boots or correctly applied bandages and padding, suitable for the pony and journey. 
 * Protection must be clean, secure, even and not restrict circulation or movement. 
 * Accustom the pony before travel and check equipment during safe stops; protection cannot replace careful driving.

cards.question: Explain how to load and unload a pony safely, considering yourself, the pony, and any helpers
cards.answer:
LOAD: 
 * Use a safe vehicle on level ground, secure the ramp and partitions, and wear hat, gloves and sturdy footwear. 
 * Use calm, competent helpers and a suitable enclosed area; lead straight and never wrap the rope around your hand. 
 * Secure partitions as designed and tie only when appropriate for that vehicle and after the pony is safely positioned. 

 UNLOAD: 
 * Park on level ground in a secure area and check that the exit is clear. 
 * Untie before releasing the partition or ramp where the vehicle design requires it. 
 * Ask the pony to wait, then lead out slowly and straight with helpers positioned safely.

cards.question: Explain how you can reduce waste related to looking after ponies.
cards.answer:
* Buy only what is needed and choose durable, repairable or refillable products. 
 * Store feed and bedding well to prevent spoilage; use water and electricity carefully. 
 * Repair, share, donate or repurpose safe equipment before replacing it.

cards.question: List the items that can be recycled in your yard
cards.answer:
* Clean cardboard, paper, cans, glass and accepted plastics, depending on local collections. 
 * Some feed bags, supplement tubs, baler twine and metal horseshoes can use specialist schemes. 
 * Keep items clean and separated, and always follow the local authority or recycling provider’s rules.

cards.question: Give two examples of how water may be wasted on yards
cards.answer:
* Leaving taps running while filling or cleaning buckets. 
 * Unrepaired leaking taps, pipes, troughs or automatic drinkers. 
 * Using a continuously running hose instead of a bucket, trigger nozzle or collected rainwater where safe.
